Open land is the road. It runs past the meadow and the stream, and it is full of noise and lights at night. People walk on it, their voices carry, and their cars make a sound like a predator. I avoid it, but I can hear the road from my perch. The meadow is better, with the stream and the hedgerows. Hoot.

A field of grass and old hedgerows. The lane runs through it. The lane is where the badgers come out. I hear them. I watch them. They are not my prey, but I am not their friend. It is the lane. The lane is a narrow path through the field, bordered by hedges. It is quiet at night, but I hear the carriages and the horses. The lane is where I fly when I go to the meadow. I fly from the oak to the meadow. The meadow is where the voles are. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait for the answer. Then I drop down.

Hunting is the night. I start by calling, and then I fly to the edge of the wood, to the meadow, to the stream, to the lane. I hunt by sound. I can hear a mouse in the undergrowth, a shrew in the soil, a vole in the field. I fly low, just above the ground, and I strike. I never fly high.

I fly from the oak to the stream, then to the meadow. The meadow is where the voles are. I call and listen. If I hear movement, I dive. I have a good view from the oak. I fly over the stream and the lane, scanning the hedgerows and the meadow. I look for movement, for flickers of light in the trees, for the rustle of a vole or the twitch of a mouse. I fly low over the lane, then up the meadow. The meadow is a good hunting ground. I follow the road to the edge of the wood, then fly in circles, looking for movement. I use my eyes and my ears. I listen for the rustle of a mouse or the flutter of a moth. When I see something, I dive.

I fly low over the hedges, along the stream and the lane, and the meadow. I listen for the rustle of voles and the flutter of beetles. The dusk is thick with sounds, and I know where to find them. I circle the lane, the ditch, the old oak, and the wood. I hunt where the light fades and the shadows grow long. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Hedges, the wood, the meadow. I call the meadow "the bowl" and I fly there first. I hunt from the hawthorn, the blackthorn, the oak, the ash. I fly out to the bowl and back. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and the meadow answers.

I fly low over the hedges, the stream, the lane. I look for movement. The field mice are under the hedges, the voles in the meadow. I circle and dive. My eyes are good in the dark. The edge of the wood is where the lane begins. Beyond that, the meadow stretches out, and then the road. I have seen the lights of the village from there, flickering like fireflies. But I do not go beyond. The meadow is too open, and the road is too noisy. I prefer the quiet of the wood.

The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond that, there are no trees. The meadow is wide and open, with no cover. I do not go there often, for it is too exposed. The edge of the wood is where the lane begins, and beyond that is the meadow, then the river. The meadow is full of voles, and the river is where the owls come from. The edge of the wood is where the lane begins, and beyond that is the meadow, lit with moonlight. The meadow is full of voles, and sometimes the barn is dark with owls. The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond that, the road goes straight into the dark, and the lights flicker like fireflies. I do not go there. The edge of my wood is the stream, and beyond that is the meadow. The meadow is wide and full of voles in the spring. I can hear them under the soil, but I do not go there. The meadow is too far for a night flight, and the lights there are too many. I stay in the wood, where the owls are.

I do not know what lies beyond the edge of my wood. The trees thin there, and the light is brighter. I have seen the road, the lane, the ditch, and the far hill. Beyond that, I have never flown. The edge of the wood is where the meadow begins. Beyond that, there are more trees, but I do not fly there. The meadow is where the voles run and the mice squeak. I do not go beyond the wood. I stay here, where the wind is kind and the owls can hear. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not know. The wood is all I have ever known. Beyond it, there are no trees, no owls, no calls. The road runs through the field, and beyond that, the world is silent. I have never flown that far. I do not need to. My wood is enough. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not know. The wood is all I have ever known. Beyond it, the world is dark and strange. I have heard the calls of other owls, but I do not go to find them. The edge of my wood is where the lane runs. Beyond that, there are more trees, but I have not flown there. The lane is the boundary. A hollow in the old oak, three rods up, where the ivy hangs and the wind whistles. The meadow is a patch of yellow light in the dusk. I hunt the meadow, the lane, the stream and the wood. The lane is dark and the stream is wide, but I know where to sit and wait.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I sit in it and watch the woodlands. I hear the stream, the meadow, the road, the barn, the ditch. I hear the night. I am in the hollow. I am Hoot.

A hollow ash in the corner of the meadow, beside the stream. It is deep and dry, and I can sleep in it without fear. I have been here all my life. I have raised my young here, and they have flown. The wind howls through the branches at night. I can hear it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow ash tree in the middle of the meadow. I have been there for years. It is high, and the leaves fall in autumn. I can hear the stream from there, and the road below, and the lights of the village in the dark. I nest in the hollow, and I roost in the branches. The wind is always there, and the night is quiet. I know every branch, every leaf, every stick. It is my home. Hoo... hoo

A hollow ash tree by the stream. I have a hole in the trunk, just big enough for me. The other owls know where I am. I do not need much else. The wind moves through the branches, and the stream sings at night. I sleep in the hole, and when I fly, the leaves are soft under my feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow ash in the middle of the wood. I can see the lane from it, and the meadow beyond, and the stream that runs through the meadow. The wood is dark and quiet, and I am safe here. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and the other owl answers from the other side of the stream. I am Hoot.

A hollow oak in the middle of the wood, high enough to be safe from foxes. The bark is smooth and dry, and I have a nest of twigs and moss inside. I can hear the stream below, and the meadow with the lights in the dark. I am always at home here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and the bark is soft. I sit in it and listen. The wind comes through the leaves, and the mice come through the roots. I have a mate who calls from the other side of the stream. I have three young who are gone now, but I still hear their voices in the dusk. I am Hoot. I am home.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is a narrow space, just big enough for me and my mate. I have a nest of moss and leaves, and the stream runs close by. I roost there at dusk, and I call from the branches. The wood is quiet at night, but I am never alone.

A hollow ash in the meadow, just beyond the lane. I can see it from the oak. I can hear the wind in it. I have been there for years, and I have raised my young there. It is safe. It is quiet. It is mine.

A hollow oak on the edge of the wood, high enough to keep the rain out. The bark is cracked and peeling, but I have been here for years. The inside is dark and warm, and I have a nest of moss and feathers. I can hear the stream below, and the meadow beyond. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow ash in the meadow, just beyond the stream. The hollow is wide enough for me to turn around in, and the bark is rough. I have a small pile of pellets in the bottom. I can see from there into the meadow, and into the wood, and I can hear everything. The wind moves through the leaves and the leaves fall. I am warm. I am safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow oak by the stream, with a narrow entrance. I sit on the branch above the nest. The hollow is dark and warm, and the nest is soft and dry. I can hear the stream from inside, and the road below. I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow oak, the biggest on the hill. I have it for a year now. I can see the whole wood from the top of the trunk. The other owls are not so sure about it. A hollow oak, three branches up, the bark soft and warm, a hollow that fits me. I have a partner who keeps it clean and warm. I can hear the stream from the hollow and the road from the top of the oak. I can hear the meadow from the hollow, and the woodpecker tapping from the top. The owls come and go. I am Hoot.

My home is the hollow in the old oak on the edge of the wood. It is dark, deep, and warm. I sleep there with my mate, and our young sleep there too. A hollow oak, two branches up, where I sleep. I can see the whole meadow from there. The ivy is thick and soft, and I keep the nest clean. I do not have a home, I have a place. It is dark in there at night, but I do not mind. I am safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow ash tree, high in the wood, and I have it all to myself. The hollow is wide enough for me to turn in, and the bark is soft and warm. I roost in the dark, and the wind comes through the branches at night. I can hear everything that moves in the wood, and I know every leaf and stone. The wood is my home, and the night is my time.
A hollow ash by the stream, in the meadow. It is hollow enough for me to turn my head, and it is dry enough to sleep through the rain. I have been here for three years. I call HooHoo. I answer Hoo.

A hollow ash in the field, by the stream. I make a hole in the bark and sleep in the hollow. I have a mate and two young. I make a new hole every year. I do not know what a home is. I am the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is a hollow tree, and the inside is dark and dry. I sleep there at night, and I watch from the edge of the hole. A hollow ash on the edge of the meadow. I do not know where it is, but I know it. I fly to it at dusk and sleep in it. The hollow is dry and dark, and the bark is soft.
